In short. These are the conditions for every Landfall small-group tour: what you pay, when, and what comes back if plans change.
A deposit of 20 % of the tour price holds your place. The balance is due 60 days before departure. If you book inside 60 days, the full price is due when you book.
More than 60 days before departure: we refund everything except the deposit, or move the deposit to another date once.
60 to 30 days: we refund 50 % of the tour price.
Fewer than 30 days: no refund, unless we resell your place.
A departure is confirmed once two travellers have booked. If we have to cancel a tour, you choose between a full refund and another date.
Guides change a route when weather, sea or a closed path make the plan unsafe. A changed day is not grounds for a refund. A lost day is, in proportion.
Travel insurance that covers the activities on your tour is required. Tell us before you book about anything that affects how far you can walk, swim or climb a ladder.

Our Californian tour covers one road: Highway 1 between Monterey and Morro Bay, the stretch known as Big Sur. It is about a hundred and fifty kilometres of cliffs, redwood canyons and very few buildings. People drive it in a day. We take eight.

Spring is the time. From March to June the hills are green, the wildflowers are out and the fog burns off by ten. Later in the year the road fills and the grass turns gold and dry. Slides sometimes close a section in winter, and Tomás checks the road each week before a departure. He grew up in Carmel, delivered along this road for six years and has an opinion about every turnout.

sections.heading: Indonesia

blocks.text: Raja Ampat by wooden phinisi, two dives a day.

Raja Ampat is a scatter of about fifteen hundred islands off the western tip of New Guinea. Getting there takes two flights and a patient day. That distance is why the reefs look the way they do. There is no large town on the islands, and only a few boats work the strait.

We go by phinisi, a wooden two-master built in Sulawesi, with eight cabins and a dive deck. The season runs from October to April, when the sea is flat and the water clear. Sari Wulandari leads every departure. She trained as a marine biologist in Manado and treats each dive as a field class, with a fish list and a quiet rule about what not to touch.

sections.heading: Italy

blocks.text: The high lakes and passes of the Dolomites, hut to hut.

In Italy we do one thing: the Dolomites, on foot, from hut to hut. The range is in the far north-east, closer to Innsbruck than to Rome, and the valleys speak Italian, German and Ladin. The paths are old and well marked, the huts are family houses with proper kitchens, and the rock turns pink for ten minutes at the end of a clear day.

The season is short. The high passes hold snow into June and the huts close in early October. September is the month we like most: settled weather, larch beginning to turn and room at the tables. Marco has guided here for twenty-six years and still carries the coffee pot to the top of every pass.

sections.heading: Maldives

blocks.text: Sandbanks, manta season and a week without shoes.

Most people see the Maldives from a resort jetty. We stay on Dharavandhoo, a local island in Baa Atoll with a school, a mosque, a football pitch and a handful of family guesthouses. The atoll is a protected biosphere reserve, and Hanifaru Bay inside it is the reason to come.

When the tide and the plankton line up, manta rays feed in the bay in long chains, and you float above them with a mask and a snorkel. Tanks are not allowed. Between visits there are sandbanks that appear at low tide, a reef with turtles a short swim from the beach, and very little else to do. Local islands serve no alcohol, and dress is modest in the village. Nobody wears shoes.
May to November for mantas, November to April for calm seas

01 · The place

Most people see the Maldives from a resort jetty. We stay on Dharavandhoo, a local island in Baa Atoll with a school, a mosque, a football pitch and a handful of family guesthouses. The atoll is a protected biosphere reserve, and Hanifaru Bay inside it is the reason to come.

When the tide and the plankton line up, manta rays feed in the bay in long chains, and you float above them with a mask and a snorkel. Tanks are not allowed. Between visits there are sandbanks that appear at low tide, a reef with turtles a short swim from the beach, and very little else to do. Local islands serve no alcohol, and dress is modest in the village. Nobody wears shoes.

blocks.text: How do I book a place?
Send the form on the plan-a-trip page or call us. A planner replies within a day, holds your place for 72 hours and sends a booking link. Nothing is charged until you confirm.
What do I pay, and when?
A deposit of 20 % holds your place. The balance is due 60 days before departure. The price on the tour page is the price you pay. There is no booking fee and no local payment.
What if I need to cancel?

More than 60 days before departure we refund everything except the deposit, or move the deposit to another date once. Inside 60 days the refund depends on what we can recover from boats and rooms. The full table is on the booking conditions page.
Do you run a tour if only a few people book?
Yes. A departure is confirmed once two travellers have booked, and we do not cancel for low numbers after that.
How fit do I need to be?
Each tour page gives the longest day. As a rule, if you can walk three to four hours with breaks you can join any walking tour. The boat trips ask only that you are steady on a ladder.
Can I come on my own?
About half of our travellers do. Rooms and cabins are shared with one other traveller unless you ask for a single. Singles cost extra where they exist. Huts, bothies and boats have none.
Tell us when you book. Vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free are no trouble on any tour. In bothies and on boats the cook plans every meal in advance, so we need to know two weeks ahead.
Within one working day, usually sooner. Planners are at their desks Monday to Friday, nine to six, Lisbon time.
Can I talk to someone who has done the tour?
Yes. Every planner has travelled the routes they sell. Say which tour you are thinking about and we put you through to the right person, or to the guide when they are not in the hills.
I am already booked. Who do I contact?
Reply to your booking email or call the number on it. In the two weeks before departure you also get your guide's mobile number.

blocks.text: Grew up on a croft above the Sound of Mull and has walked every glen we use, most of them in the rain.

Calum grew up on a croft above the Sound of Mull, the youngest of four, and left at eighteen to work on fishing boats out of Oban. He came back to the hills in his thirties, trained as a mountain leader and joined Landfall in its first year. He has led most of our Scottish departures since, in every month of the year.

He plans by the weather, not the brochure. If the cloud is down on the ridge he will take you along the shore instead and tell you why it is the better day. He cooks on the bothy trips, carries a spare pair of gloves for whoever forgot theirs and plays the whistle badly when asked. He lives in Oban with a collie called Skerry.

sections.heading: Eleni Vardaki

blocks.text: Her grandmother ran the bakery in Apollonia. She knows which path is open and whose table has room.

Eleni was born in Apollonia, on Sifnos, where her grandmother ran the village bakery for forty years. She studied archaeology in Athens, worked two summers on a dig on Despotiko and came home when she realised she liked the walk to the site more than the trench.

She has guided for Landfall since 2013 and leads both of our Greek tours: the walking week on Sifnos and the sailing week through the western Cyclades. She knows which paths were cleared this spring, which chapel has the key under the stone and whose kitchen is open on a Monday. She will order for the table unless you stop her. In winter she presses olives with her father and mends the stone walls along the paths we use.

sections.heading: Marco De Luca

blocks.text: A certified alpine guide for twenty-six years. He still carries the coffee pot.

Marco was born in Cortina and has been a certified alpine guide for twenty-six years. Before Landfall he spent a decade leading climbers on the big walls of the Dolomites, then decided he preferred the people who walk between the huts and stop to look.

He joined us in 2011 and built the lakes and passes route himself, hut by hut, mostly by asking the families who run them what they wished visitors knew. He speaks Ladin with the hut keepers and switches without noticing. He carries a moka pot and a small stove in his pack and makes coffee at the top of every pass, whatever the weather. On the free afternoon he sets up a rope under the Cinque Torri for anyone who wants to try the rock.

sections.heading: Sari Wulandari

blocks.text: Marine biologist first, guide second. She will name every fish and tell you which ones to leave alone.

Sari trained as a marine biologist in Manado and spent four years counting fish on survey lines in the Dampier Strait before she led her first dive group. She joined Landfall in 2017. She still sends her counts to the university each season, and guests are welcome to help.

She leads our two reef trips. From October to April she is on the phinisi in Raja Ampat. From May she moves to Baa Atoll in the Maldives for the manta season, where the work is done with a snorkel and a tide table. On both she hands out a fish list on the second day and gives a short talk most evenings. Her one rule is simple: look as long as you like, touch nothing.

blocks.text: Drove Highway 1 as a delivery driver before he guided on it. Knows every turnout worth the stop.

Tomás grew up in Carmel and spent six years driving a delivery van along Highway 1, from Monterey to the last ranch before San Simeon. He learned the road by its gates and its turnouts, and the people by what they ordered.

He started guiding for Landfall in 2019. He drives the van himself, which means the stops are his: a bluff with no sign, a bakery that sells out by nine, a bend where condors ride the wind on a clear afternoon. He is a patient birder and a fast cook, and he sets the table for the beach dinner while the group walks down to the arch. He will not promise you a condor. He will tell you his count for the season.

hero.subtitle: Why every walking day in Greece ends with lunch at four, and what to order when it does.

image.alt: A basket of fruit on a stone table above the sea

sections.heading: The table at the end of the path

blocks.text: The table at the end of the path
Why every walking day in Greece ends with lunch at four, and what to order when it does.
On the first day of every walking week somebody asks me when lunch is. I say four. They laugh, and at one o'clock they stop laughing.

It is not a trick. On the islands the working day used to end when the heat made work foolish. People ate their main meal then, in the shade, and slept after it. The paths we walk were built for that day. They run from a village to a field, a chapel or a cove, and they take a morning.

So we walk the morning. We start at eight with coffee and a piece of bread, carry fruit and water, and reach the sea by one or two. Then we swim. Hunger after a swim is a different thing from hunger at a desk.
My grandmother said a table by the sea needs three things: shade, bread and nobody looking at the time.
Let the kitchen decide the fish. Ask what came in that morning and take it grilled, with lemon and nothing else.

Order chickpeas if it is Sunday. On Sifnos they go into the wood oven on Saturday night in a clay pot and come out at noon. Order the caper salad anywhere, and the small fried cheese pies when you see them.
Order less than you think. Plates are for the table, not for one person, and more will arrive whether you ask or not.
Nobody walks after lunch. The bags have gone ahead. You take a nap, or the slow road back through the village when the light turns. Dinner, if you want one, is at nine and it is small.
By the fourth day most guests have stopped asking the time. That is when I know the week is working.

hero.heading: What a night in a bothy is actually like
hero.subtitle: No power, one stove and the best sleep of the year. A plain account for people who have never tried it.

image.alt: A stone room with a stove and a lamp-lit bed

sections.heading: What a night in a bothy is actually like

blocks.text: What a night in a bothy is actually like
No power, one stove and the best sleep of the year. A plain account for people who have never tried it.

A bothy is a stone hut in the hills that nobody owns in the way you own a house. The door is not locked. There is a fireplace or a stove, a sleeping platform, sometimes a table. That is the whole list.
People ask me what it is like before they book the winter trip. This is the plain version.
You walk in. There is no road to any of the bothies we use, and the shortest approach is an hour and a half. In January the light goes at four, so we aim to be at the door by two.
On our trips the second guide has gone ahead with the wood and the food. You come round the last bend and there is a lit window and smoke. People go quiet at that point. I still do.

Boots off at the door. The room is warm near the stove and cold by the far wall, and you learn within ten minutes where to sit. Supper is soup, then something heavy, then tea. There is no signal, so nobody looks at a phone after the first hour.
The first night, people talk until ten. The second night they are asleep by half past eight, and they are happier for it.
We play cards. Someone always reads aloud from the bothy book, where walkers have left notes for fifty years.

You sleep on a wooden platform on a thick mat, in a bag rated well below zero. It is dark in a way most people have forgotten. If you go outside at midnight, and you should, the stars are close and the cold catches in your nose.
In the morning the stove is lit again before you are up. Porridge, sweep the floor, carry out everything you carried in. Then the door is pulled shut for whoever comes next.

hero.subtitle: One day pack, two pairs of socks a day and nothing made of cotton. The list our guides send their own families.

image.alt: A path along dry hills above a blue sea at golden hour

sections.heading: What to pack for a walking week

blocks.text: What to pack for a walking week
One day pack, two pairs of socks a day and nothing made of cotton. The list our guides send their own families.

Every walking tour we run moves your main bag for you. That changes what packing means. You are not choosing what you can carry for a week. You are choosing what you want on your back for five hours and what can wait in the van.

A day pack of twenty to twenty-five litres with a hip belt. Inside it: a waterproof jacket, whatever the forecast says. A warm layer. Water, at least a litre and a half. Lunch, which we hand out at breakfast. Sun cream and a hat. A small dry bag for your phone.
That is all. If the pack weighs more than five kilos, something in it belongs in the other bag.
Boots or trail shoes you have already walked fifty kilometres in. This matters more than anything else on the list. New boots are the main reason people sit out a day.
Two pairs of socks for each walking day, wool or a wool mix. Change at lunch. It sounds fussy, and it is the difference between a blister on day three and none.
Nobody has ever told me they wished they had brought a third pair of trousers. Plenty have wished for a second pair of dry socks.
Cotton, in any layer that touches skin. It holds water and stays cold. Jeans. A full wash bag. More than one book. An umbrella, unless you are going to Greece, where it makes a good sunshade.
Leave the drone. Leave the laptop if you can bear to.

For Scotland, add a midge net from late May and waterproof trousers all year. For the Dolomites, a sheet sleeping bag for the huts. For Greece, swimming things in the day pack, always, because the path ends at the sea.

sections.heading: When to go where: our calendar, month by month

blocks.text: When to go where: our calendar, month by month
Twelve months, six countries and the two weeks in each when the place is at its best.
We run tours in six countries and we do not run any of them all year. Each has a few weeks when the weather, the light and the crowds line up. This is how the year looks from our planning wall.

January and February belong to the Cairngorms. The snow is firm, the bothies are empty and the days are short enough that nobody minds an early night. It is also the calm season in Raja Ampat, where the phinisi sails from October to April.
March to early June is Big Sur. The hills are green, the fog lifts by ten and Highway 1 is quiet. In May the west coast of Scotland opens, before the midges and with light until eleven.
If you can travel in only one month, make it May. Four of our six countries are open, and none of them is crowded.

From late May the mantas gather in Baa Atoll, and the Hebrides are at their calmest for the boat. June is for Greece: warm sea, open paths, room at the table. We stop in July and August, when the islands are hot and full.
The Dolomites start in late June, once the passes are clear of snow, and the huts stay open into early October.
September is the second spring. Greece again, the Highland coast again, and the Dolomites with the larch turning. In October the boat goes back to Raja Ampat and the year starts over.

A few rules of thumb. Book winter bothies by October and summer boats by February, because both are small. Ask us about the week either side of a school holiday. And if your dates are fixed, tell us the dates first and the place second. There is nearly always somewhere good to go.

sections.heading: Why we stop at twelve travellers

blocks.text: Why we stop at twelve travellers
A coach holds fifty. Our groups end at twelve. The reasons are a table, a van and a bothy floor.
Every tour on this site has the same number at the top: twelve travellers at most. People ask whether that is a marketing line. It is closer to a piece of arithmetic.

Twelve people fit around one table. That sounds small, and it decides most of a trip. At one table there is one conversation, or two, and nobody eats with their back to the group. At thirteen you need a second table, and the group quietly becomes two groups.

Twelve fit in one van with a window each. Twelve fit on the sleeping platform of the bothies we use, with the two guides by the door. The trawler in the Hebrides has twelve berths. The family rooms on Sifnos come to twelve beds if we take the whole house.

A smaller group costs more per person. The guide's wage, the van and the boat are split twelve ways instead of forty. We would rather say that plainly than hide it. It is the main reason our prices are what they are.
A guide can learn twelve names by the first lunch. After that it is a group of people, not a headcount.
It also means some departures fill quickly, and we do not add a second van when they do. We add a second date.

With twelve, the plan can bend. If one person is slow on a climb, the group waits and nobody is late for anything. If the weather turns, we can change the day over breakfast, because twelve people can be told in one sentence.
Sometimes a tour runs with five or six. We do not cancel for small numbers once two people have booked. Those are often the departures guests write to us about afterwards.

Small cabins, bare feet and a toilet with instructions. A plain guide for people who have never slept afloat.
Half the people who join the Cyclades week have never slept on a boat. They ask the same five questions on the quay, so here are the answers before you pack.
The boat is small, and that is fine
Your cabin is a bed with a door. There is room to stand in part of it and a shelf for a soft bag. Hard suitcases do not fit anywhere, so please do not bring one.
You will not be in the cabin much. Life is on deck and in the cockpit, under the shade, with your feet up. By the second day people leave their shoes in a basket and forget them.
The toilet has a pump and a short list of rules. The skipper explains it once, with a straight face. Listen.
You do not have to do anything
Nobody has to pull a rope. If you want to, you will be shown how to steer, how to take in a sail and how to tie the three knots that hold everything on a boat.
By Wednesday someone who had never sailed is at the helm, and the skipper is asleep with one eye open.

Some people do, on the first long crossing, for an hour or two. Stay on deck, look at the horizon and eat something dry. Take a tablet the night before if you know you are prone. It passes, and it rarely comes back after day two.

A few last things. Water aboard is limited, so showers are short and mostly off the stern in the sea. Bring a hat with a strap. Bring less than you think. And when the anchor goes down in an empty bay at five in the afternoon, be the first one in.

blocks.text: Old mule paths from village to village, a swim at the end of each day and a table by the water.

This is a walking week for people who like a path more than a summit. Sifnos is small, and the old mule tracks between its villages are paved in stone, walled on both sides and shaded for some of the way. If you can walk four hours with stops, you can do all of it.

The pace is set by the heat and by lunch. We start at eight, walk until one or two, swim, and sit down to eat at four as the island does. Dinners are your own, and Eleni will tell you whose table has room. Day five is a half day.
What makes it is that it is one island, done properly. You are never in a vehicle between the first ferry and the last boat. By Thursday the baker knows your order.

sections.heading: Sandbanks of Baa Atoll

blocks.text: A week between sandbanks by dhoni, manta season in Hanifaru Bay and no shoes at all.

This is a week for swimmers, not only for divers. Hanifaru Bay is snorkel-only by law, so if you can float face down and breathe through a tube you can see everything the trip is built around. Children from ten are welcome with a parent.
The pace is slow and wet. One outing by dhoni most mornings, back for lunch, and the afternoons left open for a hammock or the house reef. Nothing starts before eight except the tide.

What makes it is the season and the stay. From May the plankton gathers in the bay and the mantas follow it in. We stay on a local island in a family guesthouse, not a resort, which is why the price is what it is and why shoulders stay covered in the village. Sari reads the tide tables each evening and picks the hour.
A short flight from Malé, then the dhoni. Shoes go in a basket and stay there for a week.

blocks.text: Highway 1 at first light, cliff walks before the crowds and dinner on the beach.

This is a road trip for people who want the coast without the driving. It suits anyone who can walk two hours on a cliff path. There are no long hikes, and you can sit out any walk with a flask and the view.

The pace follows the light, not the map. The whole road is about a hundred and fifty kilometres, and we take eight days over it. We are out early, when the fog sits in the cypress and the turnouts are empty, and off the road by mid afternoon. Three nights are in the same redwood cabins, so you unpack once in the middle.

What makes it is Tomás. He drove this road for work before he guided on it, and he knows which turnouts have no sign and a path. One evening the table is set on the sand, and the van carries the jumpers.
Meet at three, walk the bay path and eat early. Everyone is still on another clock.

blocks.text: Five short winter days between stone bothies, with a fire lit before you arrive.

This is a short winter trip for people who are curious about bothies and not sure about the cold. You need to be able to walk three hours on snow or frozen ground with a pack of about eight kilos. You do not need winter skills. We lend the kit and show you how to use it.

The days are short because the light is. We walk from nine to about two and reach the bothy with the fire already lit. The evening is soup, cards and an early night. Day three goes high only if the weather allows it.

sections.heading: The Cyclades by sailboat

blocks.text: Eight days under sail between five islands, swimming off the stern and eating where the fishermen eat.

This is a sailing week for people who have never sailed, and for people who have and miss it. Nobody has to pull a rope. Anyone who wants to steer, trim a sail or learn the knots will be handed something within the hour.

The pace depends on the wind, which is the point. Most days are two to four hours under sail, a long swim stop, and a harbour or an anchorage by late afternoon. Day five is on land. If the meltemi blows hard we change the order of the islands, not the number.

What makes it is the size of the boat. Fifteen metres, four guest cabins and a keel shallow enough for coves the ferries and day boats cannot use. Eleni eats where the fishermen eat, and on two nights that is a table with no menu.

sections.heading: Lakes and passes of the Dolomites

blocks.text: Lakes and passes of the Dolomites
Row Lago di Braies before the day trippers, cross three passes on foot and sleep in family-run rifugios.

This is a hut-to-hut walk for people who are comfortable with six hours on their feet and a few hundred metres of climb before lunch. There is no climbing and no drop you cannot walk around. If you have done a long weekend in the hills with a rucksack, you are ready.

The days are honest: between four and fifteen kilometres, three passes, and one cable car down when the knees have earned it. One afternoon is free. Bags travel by road on four days. On the others you carry what you need for the night.

What makes it is the huts and the hour on the lake. Rifugios here are family houses with a kitchen, and Marco has known most of the families for twenty years. We row Lago di Braies at first light, when the water is flat and the car park is empty.

sections.heading: Sea lochs of the Hebrides

blocks.text: A converted trawler, seven sea lochs, otters at breakfast and a skipper from Stornoway.
This is a slow week on a boat for people who would rather watch a shoreline than tick off sights. No sailing skill is asked for. You need to be steady on a ladder and happy in a small cabin.

The pace is the tide's. We move for two or three hours most days, anchor in a different sea loch each night and go ashore by dinghy when there is something to walk to. One crossing, to the Shiant Isles, is open water and can be lumpy. If the forecast is poor we stay inside, and nobody minds.

What makes it is the trawler and the people on her. She fished out of Stornoway for thirty years before the refit, and the skipper worked on her as a boy. Twelve berths, one long table and a wheelhouse you are welcome in. Otters most mornings. Signal almost never.

sections.heading: The Highland coast on foot

blocks.text: Six days from glen to sea cliff with twelve travellers, a stove in every tent and a guide from Oban.

This is a walking tour for people who walk at weekends, not for mountaineers. The longest day is fourteen kilometres on a shore path and the shortest is five. A boat or a van carries the bags, so you carry water, lunch and a jacket.

The pace is unhurried on purpose. We start after breakfast, stop when the light is good and reach each night's bed with time to sit outside before dinner. Day four is half free: the cliff path early, then nothing until supper unless you want it.

What makes it is where you sleep. Canvas with a stove in Glen Etive, a cabin on the loch, the inn at Ardnamurchan and a dome under the Cuillin. Calum has walked this coast since he was a boy and plans each day around the weather that morning. Bring waterproofs and expect to use them.
Meet in Glasgow at nine, drive north and walk the last hour to camp. Dinner is on the deck.

sections.heading: A reef week in Raja Ampat

blocks.text: A reef week in Raja Ampat
Nine days on a wooden phinisi, two dives a day and a marine biologist on board.

This is a dive trip for certified divers with at least twenty logged dives. Some sites have current, and you should be at ease with a drift and a safety stop in blue water. Non-divers are welcome and can snorkel every site but two.

The boat sets the pace. Two dives on most days, one before breakfast and one after lunch, with long hours in between for sleep, books and Sari's talks on deck. Days four and six are lighter, with time ashore.

What makes it is the reef and the person explaining it. Raja Ampat sits in the middle of the Coral Triangle, and one dive here can show two hundred kinds of fish. Sari has studied these reefs since university. You get her fish list on day two. By day eight most people have ticked a hundred and know which ones to leave alone.
Meet at the harbour at four. Cabins, a safety talk and the first dinner on deck as we leave port.
